I want to give this an honest review, because although I enjoyed it and the game does have a lot of potential, there are some setbacks to it as well.

Positives:
-The gameplay is fun and paced well. It never felt boring or slow, and the storyline was intriguing and kept me interested throughout.
-The detective work was interesting, but not too challenging. Other than [spoiler] the bomb defusing puzzle which was super annoying and convoluted out of nowhere and with a time limit that made it even worse [/spoiler] I could progress easily without feeling like it was too simple.
-The game's ui was easy to use and had nice to look at.

Negatives:
-It's well written, but really short. As you can tell from my playtime, it moved super quickly. While the story was still satisfying for the most part, it felt like it ended prematurely due to the short length. I would have liked to have seen at least a few more days worth of gameplay.
-The ending felt, to me, very unsatisfying. [spoiler] Although I'm sure, given the after credits scene, this is meant to be a cliff hanger for the next game, the way it ended just left me feeling like all the work I had done was meaningless and therefore the game had been meaningless. That's not to say the ending was all bad or should be completely changed. But, for example, if it had ended with one person being apprehended, or something similar to give some sense of conclusion, it would have been a lot better. As it is, I finished it somewhat annoyed. As if I had wasted all that effort for no reward, and an unfinished storyline. [/spoiler] This criticism is somewhat of a personal opinion, I know, but it really soured my view of the game at the end. Which was a shame, because up until that very moment I was super engrossed in the story and really enjoying it.

Overall, I enjoyed the gameplay and story right up until the final minute. So I would recommend the game, if you got it on sale or don't mind that it is very short, and you aren't put off by the thought of an abrupt ending. I think this studio did a great job producing it though and telling a story, and look forward to their next game. I only hope their next ending will feel a bit more satisfying for the player.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 98:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

[i] The Operator [/i] casts you not as a hero in the field, but as the analyst—the voice behind the computer—supporting agents from the shadows. It’s a fascinating setup and a fresh twist on crime-solving games, and usually almost always lives up to its potential!

🖥[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Authentic "operator" fantasy. You monitor missions from your desk, field phone calls, look through mysterious documents, and scrub through CCTV footage. 

[*] Diverse tools. The game gives you a chem scanner, facial recognition database, image enhancement tech, and document search systems. For example, in one mission, you identify a suspect by cross-referencing a blurry security camera with an equally blurry security footage of his car and license plate. That kind of detective work feels cool. You feel smart when it works.

[*] Great use of puzzles under pressure. A standout moment has you guiding a field agent through bomb defusal. You have to analyze chemicals, check your reference files, and read out step-by-step instructions—all while the timer ticks down. These time-sensitive missions are where the game shines.

[*] Well-done audio design. The UI clicks, radio static, and phone calls all contribute to a grounded, late-'90s thriller vibe. The voice acting is low-key but sells the scenario well, especially during moments of stress or confusion.

[*] No filler. It’s tight and focused. No wandering, no padding. You’re thrown into the action quickly and missions move at a brisk pace.
[/list]

[b]🧾 Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Flat characters. The field agents and mysterious hacker HAL are more archetypes than flesh-and-blood. They push the story forward, but rarely surprise

[*] Choices don’t matter much. There are dialogue branches, but most are cosmetic. Whether you’re professional or snarky, or even whether you succeed or fail at certain puzzles, the game mostly funnels you into the same story beats.

[*] Abrupt ending. The game ends just as things get interesting. HAL’s storyline ramps up, then vanishes. You barely get to dig into the conspiracy or see the consequences of your actions. It feels like a miniseries that ends on episode three.
[/list]

4/5

If you're a fan of games like 'Papers, Please' then you should check this game out.

Gameplay is really fun, having you find connections between cases and uncovering clues to unlock encrypted drives. Story was great, and definitely kept me engaged through the whole game. Some twists are a bit obvious, while other ones completely shocked me, though it made the experience better.

My only complaint is that this wasn't longer with more stuff to do. There's a specific timed mission you have near the end involving Agent Pendell that's probably the highlight in regards to problem-solving in this game. I was also really saddened by the ending, so I hope a sequel in the works to resolve all the questions that came up after that.

This game has an interesting premise and it has been made well. The graphics are good and the audio is top notch in my books.

But unfortunately it's... hmm, how should I say it... easy? Or not even that, hand-heldy! Like, it doesn't really let you do much anything of worth outside of one high stakes scene that is timed. But that it not what 99% of the game is.

It's kinda like this game is backwards from what you would expect from a logic puzzle game. It's the Agents or other people that call you aka the NPC's aka the game itself that do most of the detective work. And you, the player, are the computer whose job is to do the tedious work of checking. You get one single question to answer from the field agent and the answer is never that hard to find. In fact it's almost never necessary to collect and compile information as an active researcher and there's basically no need to take notes. Most of the times you just click on the right, kinda obvious document and do the thing and then answer so the plot may thiccen.

And it's not like the setting of the game, you being the computer guy helping detectives in the field means it has to be boring. There could have been more you could do. But most of the intrigue in this game comes from chat interactions, not from actual action you get to do.

Like for example, there are two things that could have been so fun to get to use as active participant, as part of a larger puzzle YOU need to solve yourself, the chemical analysis software and the bomb defusing manual, that only get one use. And also, no love for the vehicle database, just for people database. But like, just being able to do more than to just find out an answer to one question at a time, being able to take notes and to make actual deductions? Would have been fun. Think of Mainlining as an example.

It's just that, there is so much promise. This game was instant purchase for me as soon as I found out about it, as a fan of mystery and "hacking" genre of games. But it just didn't really deliver what I hoped for. And I'm kinda bummed about it.

review_text_raw:
This is a pretty solid game, at least the first time around. I've only been through it once, but I am curious about how it will be after a few runs. It's definitely a bit shorter than I thought (this run was around 3 hours), and while I didn't do much research on it before buying it (other than reading the tags and brief parts of the description), it seemed a bit different than what I expected. I was kind of thinking you'd go through and help solve multiple cases, and just keep going that way with increasing difficulty and depth as you continue playing. It's not that. It sort of starts that way, but doesn't stay that way for long. It's VERY linear as far as I can tell, and while I think there are different outcomes based on player inputs, I have yet to try that. It's not the investigation game it's labeled as. It's still well put together and thought out, but I felt a little bit misled, as there is really only one single "case" that you're working on as the player, it just happens to include a few other cases that you work on in the tutorial stages. 

Without spoiling it, I think it's a good game, though I don't know if I would pay full price for it. I think if you could get it for under $10 USD it would be a much better value, personally. But, we'll see how it goes on the replay-ability of the game and that might change. I'm curious how different actions and responses affect the outcome of the game for sure. 

Soundtrack really buffed this game a lot too, it was really well timed and well orchestrated. 

My main complaint is some of the cutscenes are ridiculously long for what their substance is. There is basically no substance to most of them, it's just some sound effects and maybe the occasional spot of dialogue.

As someone else said in their review, it scratched an itch I didn't know I had, but I would've been much more excited to see some real investigating. Like phasmophobia, but you're the computer geek at this government intelligence agency. If you play through the first hour or so, you'll see sort of what I mean by that.

review_text_raw:
I don't think this game is quite what I expected. It's a style of game I'd love to see more of. But while I still mostly enjoyed my time with it, I'm left wanting more.

The story itself is interesting and has enough of those classic thriller movie twist and turns to keep you engaged throughout. Role-playing the "man in the chair" is pretty fun, and you have a few moments that deliver on that promise, at least from a narrative standpoint.

After playing this through once, you'd think the game had multiple endings. You are left wondering if maybe there's some way to correct your mistakes and change the outcome. That is not the case. The ending is pretty bleak, comes pretty quickly (the game itself only being a few hours long at most), and doesn't bring the story to a proper close. I can do without a "good ending", but there's a disappointing lack of closure here.

Broadly speaking, The Operator fails to deliver on the use of "detective skills" it says you'll need in the game's description. You definitely interact with a computer and run a few faux-terminal commands, but most of the time you're just finding a name or a face by clicking the a button that Zoom-Enhances a video CSI style. It sure looks like you're doing the work, but none of it is very challenging and it all feels a little superficial.

There's maybe one section that raises the difficulty and that's because it puts you on a timer and forces you to read an instruction manual. It's the first and only challenging moment the game offers. It was actually a pretty good moment, and the game could have done with a few more scenes this.

I'd not recommend this game to fans of puzzle games who are looking for a challenge, but it's still a fun journey if you want to spend a few hours in the world of a thriller movie. Just don't expect a satisfying ending.

6/10 - Soft recommendation (Buy on sale).

This is a very short game, you'll be done in 3 hours if you're competent at basic puzzles ~ less if you spam the hint feature.

This is an investigation game, where you're an operator in the FDI (or FBI really), and the investigative features boil down to clicking on images and connecting evidence when asked to do so. There's the odd puzzle, but it isn't particularly difficult ~ the hardest part is a timed segment, which you can get around by pausing the game, as all the information remains on screen anyway.

Really, you're here to play this for the storyline, which is a fairly predictable conspiracy laced, X-files, deep-state mystery. The twists are fairly obvious, but the execution of the story beats/elements are lacking. 

It feels as if the story would have better served from being a bit longer, given more time to stew a bit. There's unnecessary padding, in full blur cut scenes that take place between each 'day', and they seem to exist either for 'atmosphere' or more cynically, just to pad the game out so you go over the 2 hour refund mark. (Your mileage may vary, they did nothing for me but waste time.)

For £10, it is... okay? At best. There's one ending, as far as I know, so there's little reason to replay the game. As a one-shot experience, it is decent, but I think it is better on a deeper sale, something around £5-7 maybe, as this is such a niche experience, it doesn't really do anything new.

If you're an X-Files fans, or someone who loves conspiracy theories, lizard people behind the scenes (or a flat-Earther, whatever), you'll be right at home here. Otherwise, it is a fairly basic investigative game that doesn't quite nail the key plot points to take it beyond being simply decent.

So it was a Sunday evening. As it sometimes happens, nothing in my library felt right. So, I went to check my wishlist to see if there was anything that would feel satisfying. I stumbled upon The Operator. And, well, let me tell you, it was everything I needed and even more. I have to say that it's rather short, but just perfect to fill out that one evening of boredom. The gameplay is relaxing for your hands yet somewhat demanding for your brain. I liked solving little puzzles and interconnections. I don't want to spoil anything, but the game gives you huge satisfaction in a few moments when you actually figure stuff out. Wouldn't say it was hard to keep up with all the clues, but I'm pretty sure I still missed some pieces of info. And man, that section when you actually had a timer on, that was really damn cool (no spoilers).

The story? Well, it's great. It kept me invested till the very end, which not every AAA game can do. I have to say that some of the plot twists were quite easy to read, but not all of them. I loved the way they conveyed the story between the work days, never seen anything like it. Sound and music are very important parts of that game, and they were done just perfectly. Nothing else to say here.

To summarize, it is a great experience (that's what I would rather call it) for one evening. If you liked Orwell games or anything else in the genre, you will definitely like this one too. Worth buying, even for full price.

This game is short around 3-4 hours, but it's very memorable. Reminds me of Orwell (the first one, which was just amazing).

The interface is retro and stilted, but you can tell that it's a design choice by the author. Behind the retro graphics of what is essentially a conspiratorial work simulator, the game stands out as a very polished experience. I have experienced no bugs. Once I knew the basic game mechanics, I didn't feel cheated in anyway by the game. If I made a mistake during gameplay, it was because I was distracted, not because the game didn't provide enough clues.

The polish of the game also stands out with the brilliant sound design. The music is spot-on with some Tool-like guitars like the song Rosetta Stoned blended with futuristic suspense tunes.

review_text_raw:
As short as it was, the heavy X-Files influences hit just right to keep me hooked. A lot of the twists were pretty obvious but nonetheless still felt satisfying to experience even when predicted which just gives more praise to the writing to be able to pull that off. The ending wasn't to my tastes, was easily the most predictable part of the story and was very deliberately cliffhangered, but it does at least fit the genre and for what it is, it was executed well.

I was also a bit disappointed in how light the puzzle elements were but there were some satisfying moments connecting the dots, and having to go through and parse the bomb defusing manual on the fly was a good bit of fun.

The sound design is just absolutely excellent. It's not exactly subtle but the shifts in tone are timed perfectly to important moments, the music in general is very fitting without being intrusive. And god damn, the clacking of keys on the keyboard and mouse clicks are absolutely DIVINE and would make top tier ASMR.

If you don't mind something leaning more towards a visual novel and like the theme, it's definitely worth the few hours to get through. Hope to see more like this in the future.

review_text_raw:
Fun game that stands out in some areas and could have been better in others.

By far the strongest aspect was the sound and music design. I really enjoyed hearing the crescendo kick in right when you discover something interesting. It was well timed, and well executed. 

The story was on the better side of good, but probably just a bit below great. I think the VAs actually did a great job and elevated the story much higher than it would have been with just text.

The puzzles were fun, but I'd say only 2-3 of them were really difficult enough to be solidly engaging rather than just enjoyable.

Finally, the length was disappointing, but not enough to ruin the rest of the experience. If anything, I'd say it's a good sign that I wanted more.

Overall, a solid 7.5/10. I wouldn't necessarily call this a puzzle game, more of a narrative thriller that uses puzzles to guide you through the plot. So understand that before you get it. Worth the price in the same way a movie is worth the price, but for most people you'll probably want to wait for a sale.

review_text_raw:
Very fun while it lasts: it's a interactive fiction where you are a intelligence agency operator trying to do your job by identifying crucial details with scripted in game calls. Not to spoil, but this involved entering key words into the correct prompt and linking information. 
Unfortunately, it only has one ending in a mostly linear path, so no matter what you do you'll pretty well get the same ending. 
but it's a fantastic short play. 
some highlights:
solve cases with database searches, evidence reviews, and crosslinking data for answers
A timed bomb defusal where you have to talk someone through not getting blown up
some espionage/live mission support for a *redacted* sting operation
some on the fly multiple choice dialogue making you second guess every option
a stellar ending. 

Sadly, it's less interactive and more fictional narrative than one would hope. 
Hopefully the sequel will have non-linear plots, side plots, and dynamic choices with more emphasis on your choices mattering and divergent paths. 

I highly recommend this to anyone who has an interest in puzzles and psedo-intelligencia government fiction/espionage thrills.
